column1: # The game's sound effects: one row per name the code plays.
# Regenerate with `python Tools/make_sfx.py`; prove the shipped wavs are what it
# writes with `--check`; audition them with `--contact`. Read the head of
# slot      the name `Audio.Sfx("...")` asks for. A fixed vocabulary - see below.
# source    path inside the pack's WAV folder (see the audio-source-pack note).
# semis     semitones to transpose. Resample-pitch, so it shifts speed too.
# head      seconds to keep. Blank keeps the whole (trimmed) clip.
# trim_db   gain trim on top of the loudness match, in dB. Blank is 0.
# lowpass   Hz. Blank is none. Takes fizz off a sample that is otherwise right.
# family    which material this belongs to, for the contact sheet's grouping.
# note      why this source, in one line.
# The slots are a fixed vocabulary: `AssetManifest.Sfxs` preloads exactly these
# names and `Tools/verify/sfxnames.py` proves the code asks for no other. Adding
# one means adding it in all three places.
# Twelve source files carry twenty slots, and the reuse is the point: a small
# palette of materials is what makes a set sound like one place rather than
# twenty samples. Where a source is used twice the two are a interval apart, so
# they read as two notes of one instrument - `tick` and `tock` are literally the
# same block of wood a fourth apart, which is what a tick and a tock are.
# Every `semis` is a pentatonic step (0, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12 and their negatives).
# The game overlaps these constantly - `lit` climbs twelve notes on one turn -
# and a pentatonic set has no semitone in it, so no two can collide into a beat.

column8: note
Every button in the game. Chosen by ear over the measurements, which is the owner's call to make.
A tone below click, cut from the same wood, so a retreat reads as downward.
Every panel opening - settings, pause, all twenty-five modals. The tap that opened it is hushed so this is the only sound.
Every tip box and info bubble. Brighter than the menu, because a bubble is smaller than a panel.
Committing to a level from the map. Its own slot rather than `unlock`, which is what it used to borrow and which nine other things still use.
Poking the critter on the home screen. Played with a wide random detune, which is what keeps a toy from getting old.

column2: BONGS - TIMERS - BELLS - (72)/BONG Clunk Hit Short 02.wav
column8: Bright at source because the game plays it at .6 pitch, and .6 of a dull sound is nothing a phone can reproduce.
The gentlest refusal in the pack, and the one clip trimmed below the rest.

A critter getting out of its cocoon. The owner picked this source by ear. It is `menu`'s clip a fifth up, which is the reuse the head of this file describes: the same block of wood struck higher, so a cocoon opening is heard as a brighter relative of a panel opening rather than as a new instrument. The bell-and-chime pair that used to play here was removed for being the loudest thing in the game, four times a chain.

A flower going off in Budburst. Its own slot rather than `pop`, which eight other things play: this one is struck thirteen times in a wave and pitched up through a chain, so it has to be the shortest and brightest thing in the set and nothing else should be tuned by it. Measured at 0.12s and a 4.7kHz centroid against `pop`'s 0.16s and 519Hz - the old sound was a wooden clunk, which is what a flower bursting into light is not.
Wood rather than glass. There is no glass in a grove.
Turning a conduit - the most-heard sound in the game. Chosen by ear over three earlier attempts; nothing in the 2-5 kHz band at all.
The other half of the turn coin-flip: the same bloop a tone up, so the two read as one action.
The same stone, longer and softer.
A mechanism rather than a chime, so the lid has weight.
